A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices support a reliable comparison, including matching retained material across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original reading-time prediction experiments, attention-head ablations and regularized GPT2 training, with additional empirical results in its appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds Gaussian-noise controls, head-interaction analyses, permutation tests and analyses of loss–PPP relationships.

M1.justification: The syntactic and copying regularization objectives, pattern-preserving head ablation and core scoring procedures are retained. PMS becomes PS without changing its definition. Gaussian noise injection is an added comparison condition, rather than a revision to the proposed suppression methods.

E1.justification: Both versions retain CC100 training, Dundee, MECO, Provo and Natural Stories reading data, and BLiMP and synthetic-sequence evaluations. The added controls and analyses use existing coverage. Brain-alignment results discussed in v2 are attributed to other studies.

E2.justification: Experiment 3 adds one comparator family: Gaussian Noise Injection, evaluated at sigma = 0.05 and 50 alongside NoReg and the existing syntactic and copying regularization variants. The original comparison methods remain.

E3.justification: v2 substantially extends Experiment 3's evaluation design by analyzing validation loss versus PPP separately before and after phase transition, using PS for transition timing except UAS for copy-suppressed models. It also introduces Gaussian-noise control settings. Figure 1 changes the reported Pythia batch size from 2,048 to 1,024; this reporting revision does not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Appendix K examines how suppressing SAS affects induction heads and how suppressing induction heads affects SAS, including downstream BLiMP and ICL behavior. Section 6 and Appendix N add analyses of loss–PPP relationships around phase transition, while Gaussian-noise controls test nonspecific perturbation. The original head ablations and suppression checks are retained.

E5.justification: Beyond the existing correlation significance reporting, v2 adds 10,000 within-word permutations for comparisons against NoReg (Appendix I/Table 3) and Fisher-z weighted pooling of correlations across models (Figure 4). These are substantial additions to statistical assessment. The permutation p-values are explicitly reported without multiple-testing correction.

E6.justification: Table 1's numerical entries are unchanged, but v2 adds Gaussian-noise outcomes, cross-head interaction findings, permutation p-values and transition-specific loss–PPP results. For example, new Figure 4 reports pooled Dundee correlations of -0.976 before transition and 0.416 afterward. Original regularization results are retained in expanded Figures 16–17.

T1.justification: The UAS attention-scale argument changes from claiming approximately 0.002 expected attention for every j > i in v1 Appendix B to averaging over j > i in v2 Appendix C. It also changes j < i to j <= i in the preceding expression. This is a limited mathematical revision; the central definitions and objectives remain.

C1.justification: The central phase-transition explanation and abstract are retained. The introduction and conclusion refine the regularization claim toward delaying the transition and PPP peak, and more explicitly favor the Dynamics Hypothesis over attributing degradation to persistent specialized heads.

C2.justification: v1 treats incomplete suppression largely as a possible explanation for residual degradation. v2 explicitly documents incomplete suppression, explains why absolute PPP comparisons must consider language-model loss, and proposes SAS scaffolding and attention competition as possible explanations of asymmetric head interactions. It also adds qualified comparisons with brain-alignment dynamics.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code/data availability link and a substantial hyperparameter table covering architecture, parameter counts, learning rate, weight decay, warmup and scheduling. It newly specifies the 0.1 breakthrough threshold and gaze-duration outcome, and documents Gaussian-noise implementation. These disclosures materially improve reproducibility without establishing changes to existing training settings.

R1.justification: The foundational related-work account remains. v2 adds discussion of brain-alignment studies by AlKhamissi et al. and Nakagi et al., supporting references for small-model research, and explicit novelty claims about studying SAS in decoder-only models and observing both specialized-head types together.

P1.justification: Experiment 3 and the conclusion are substantially rewritten around transition delay and loss–PPP relationships. The discussion gains thematic subsections, hypotheses are reorganized as 1/2a/2b, and the original absolute-PPP discussion moves into an expanded appendix structure. Terminology and explanations are also revised throughout.

P2.justification: New main Figures 3–4 replace the earlier main-text displays, which survive as expanded appendix Figures 17 and 16. v2 adds interaction and validation-loss plots and Tables 2–4, revises legends and axes, and distinguishes positive and negative significant correlations by color in Table 1. These substantially change the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens assessment of the central mechanism claim. Compared with v1's emphasis on absolute PPP improvements, it adds perturbation controls, examines loss–PPP dependence, tests statistical significance and investigates incomplete suppression directly. These additions support a more precise interpretation of transition delay and expose limits of the regularization evidence. The new implementation details also improve reproducibility. Full causal isolation remains unresolved, but the gains address important evidential and interpretive weaknesses.
